extracted.intended_audience: Reuters sports journalists and news reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Style and reporting guidelines for writing sports news copy (usage, spelling, phrasing, coverage schedules and story priorities) aimed at Reuters sports correspondents and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: units and currency conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: In boxing involving U.S. fighters and aimed at a U.S. market conversions into imperial may be added for height, weight etc. otherwise there is no need to convert in brackets. All currencies must show a conversion into dollars at first reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: convince (transitive verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: The verb is transitive and needs an object. You must convince someone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Andrew Symonds failed to convince selectors he was back to his best … not Andrew Symonds failed to convince on his return from injury. Alternative: use the adverb: Andrew Symonds batted convincingly...

rubrics_metrics.name: coolly (spelling/usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'coolly' (with two l's) as in Ronaldinho coolly tapped the ball home; not 'cooly'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: 'cooly' is incorrect; OED reference to other meanings is irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: crowd (verb agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'crowd' takes a singular verb.

rubrics_metrics.name: defeat (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A team is defeated by another, not to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: After Bolton's 2-0 defeat by Arsenal … not 'to Arsenal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: delight (transitive verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: To delight is a transitive verb and needs an object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Marat Safin delighted Russian fans with a neat chip… not 'Marat Safin delighted with a chip…'

rubrics_metrics.name: different (preposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'different from', not 'different to'.

rubrics_metrics.name: distances (athletics/swimming formatting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Express distances as: 400 metres hurdles/400 metres freestyle (metres in plural). Say: the 400-metre pool, 100-metre track etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metres is always written out, never abbreviated to 'm'. Kilometres are abbreviated to 'km'.

rubrics_metrics.name: double fault (tennis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write as two words: 'double fault'.

rubrics_metrics.name: drop shot (tennis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write as two words: 'drop shot'.

rubrics_metrics.name: disaster/tragedy (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'disaster' or 'tragedy' for sporting contests because this devalues the word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'disaster'/'tragedy' for real catastrophes (e.g. a stand falling down and crushing fans), not for losing a match.

rubrics_metrics.name: downhill (Alpine skiing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell as one word: 'downhill'.

rubrics_metrics.name: dramatic (avoid overuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: The adjective 'dramatic' is usually unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events like penalty shootouts or last-minute goals are by their nature dramatic; the word often adds little.

rubrics_metrics.name: evening/morning (time references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not refer to evening or morning games because these vary around the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use GMT time or phrasing such as 'later on Thursday' or 'earlier on Monday' instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: extra cover (cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fielding position written as two words: 'extra cover'.

rubrics_metrics.name: fast bowler (cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write as two words: 'fast bowler'. Use only for genuine speedsters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also 'pace bowler' for quick bowlers who may not be genuine fast bowlers.

rubrics_metrics.name: fears/hopes (sourcing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unattributed hopes and fears are opinions. All fears and hopes need to be sourced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Fears that Manchester United might lose their Premier League title...' should indicate who fears it, since one fan's fear may be another's hope.

rubrics_metrics.name: feet (measurement policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feet, inches and yards are used only in golf and in American sport for U.S. audiences; otherwise use metric measurements without conversions.

rubrics_metrics.name: first slip (cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fielding position: two words 'first slip'.

rubrics_metrics.name: flaunt vs flout
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Flaunt' means to display ostentatiously; 'flout' means to defy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct verb to match meaning (e.g. By flaunting your wealth you flout convention).

rubrics_metrics.name: flyhalf (rugby)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word for the rugby position: 'flyhalf'.

rubrics_metrics.name: focused (spelling/usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell 'focused' with one 's' (not 'focussed').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term is overused in sport; avoid except in quotations. Use 'concentrated' as an alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: football/soccer (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: If referring to association football for some audiences use 'soccer' at first reference as several other games around the world are known as 'football'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific with forms: American football or NFL, Aussie Rules (ARF) when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: forehand (racket sports)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word: 'forehand'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula One (capitalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Formula One' in motor racing references.

rubrics_metrics.name: fractions (formatting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to use decimals but where fractions are unavoidable they are written 4-1/2, 6-3/4 etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: free kick (soccer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write as two words: 'free kick'.

rubrics_metrics.name: girl/boy (age usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'girl' or 'boy' for anyone over 18; use 'man' or 'woman'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: team names at first reference (e.g. Fulham Ladies) are allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: goalkeeper (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word: 'goalkeeper'. 'Keeper' may be used without an apostrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand Prix (capitalization and plural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize in the title of a race or event (The Monaco Grand Prix); lower case generally when generic. The plural is 'grands prix'.

rubrics_metrics.name: grand slam (case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower case 'grand slam' in tennis and rugby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The Australian Open, first grand slam event of the year' and 'Ireland are aiming for their first grand slam for 11 years'.

rubrics_metrics.name: grasscourt (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: As an adjective, one word 'grasscourt' (e.g. The grasscourt tournament at the Queen's club). As adjective+noun, two words: 'grass courts'.

rubrics_metrics.name: group (capitalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to competition groups in upper case in copy: Group One, Group Two etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly use 'Group One' for races in horse racing.

rubrics_metrics.name: guineas (horse races)
rubrics_metrics.description: Horse race naming: '2,000 Guineas' (capitalize 'Guineas'), not '2000 guineas'.

rubrics_metrics.name: gully (cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell 'gully' without an 'e' for the cricket fielding position.

rubrics_metrics.name: halftime
rubrics_metrics.description: One word: 'halftime'.

rubrics_metrics.name: hardcourt (tennis)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word as an adjective ('the Boston hardcourt tournament'), two words as adjective/noun ('the hard courts were designed for big servers').

rubrics_metrics.name: hat-trick (hyphenation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated: 'hat-trick'.

rubrics_metrics.name: hiccup (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'hiccup', not 'hicough'.

rubrics_metrics.name: honorifics (avoid titles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use honorific titles in sports stories; use plain names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Don Bradman and Alex Ferguson, not Sir Don and Sir Alex.

rubrics_metrics.name: icon (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Icon' is banned on the sports file for describing sporting figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'icon' only in religious contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: impress (transitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'impress' transitively (needs an object).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Smith impressed selectors' (not 'Smith impressed during his two-hour innings'). The passive 'was impressive' is permissible but weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ireland (naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Ireland' rather than 'Republic of Ireland' or 'Irish Republic'.

rubrics_metrics.name: ironically (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the adverb 'ironically'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is said or done is rarely ironic; often it's merely coincidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: jargon (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid jargon; see also guidance on cliches.

rubrics_metrics.name: judoka (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'judoka' as the adjective to describe someone who plays judo.

rubrics_metrics.name: just (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Just' is often superfluous in sports stories and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'He has won one title in 23 years' not 'He has just won one title...'; 'Capriati was 14' not 'just 14'.

rubrics_metrics.name: key (avoid overuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: The adjective 'key' is overused in sports stories and usually superfluous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid phrases like 'key players', 'key positions' unless specifically necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: kickoff (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word, no hyphen: 'kickoff'.

rubrics_metrics.name: kilometres (abbreviation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'km' for kilometres, with no full point, for singular and plural.

rubrics_metrics.name: lady (gendered term usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'lady' except in the title of teams at first reference (e.g. Fulham Ladies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where organisers use 'Ladies' Championship' substitute 'women's championship'.

rubrics_metrics.name: leaderboard (golf)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word: 'leaderboard'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mostly used in golf.

rubrics_metrics.name: leave (verb usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid weak or vague uses of 'leave' where a more active, accurate verb is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace clumsy constructions like 'Two clumsy tackles left Robben suffering from torn ligaments' with 'Robben suffered torn ligaments after two clumsy tackles.'

rubrics_metrics.name: left-arm spinner (hyphenation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write with a hyphen: 'left-arm spinner' for the slow bowler in cricket.

rubrics_metrics.name: legend/legendary (avoid exaggeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confine 'legend'/'legendary' to real legends (e.g. myths); do not call sportspeople 'legend'.

rubrics_metrics.name: leg slip (cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fielding position: two words 'leg slip'.

rubrics_metrics.name: leg-spinner (cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write as 'leg-spinner' for the bowler type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ligue 1 (capitalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Ligue 1' for the French first division in soccer.

rubrics_metrics.name: like vs such as
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'such as' when offering examples; 'like' means similar to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Players such as Deco and Ricardo Carvalho...' (not 'players like Deco and Ricardo Carvalho' if giving examples). Use 'Bowlers like Andrew Flintoff, who put a lot of pressure on their leading leg...' to mean bowlers with a similar action.

rubrics_metrics.name: lineup (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word: 'lineup'.

rubrics_metrics.name: lineout (rugby)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word: 'lineout'.

rubrics_metrics.name: long-off/long-on (cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cricket fielding positions 'long-off' and 'long-on' use hyphens.

rubrics_metrics.name: major (avoid as adjective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'major' as an adjective (major signing, major importance) because it is hackneyed and often superfluous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: in golf, the four biggest tournaments are known as the 'majors'.

rubrics_metrics.name: masterful vs masterly
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Masterly' means very skilful and is usually the intended word; 'masterful' means imperious or domineering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'masterly' in sports contexts (e.g. 'Tiger Woods put on a masterly display...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Masters Series (capitalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Masters Series' for leading men's tennis tournaments (e.g. Rome Masters Series).

rubrics_metrics.name: match point (tennis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write as two words: 'match point'.

rubrics_metrics.name: medal (do not verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Medal' should not be used as a verb; competitors win medals, they do not 'medal'.

rubrics_metrics.name: metres (spelling and usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out 'metres' in copy (use British English '-re' spelling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the 100 metres backstroke'. If multiple races are mentioned, 'metres' can be dropped after first reference. No need to convert to feet/yards except in golf and U.S. sport.

rubrics_metrics.name: mid-on/mid-off/mid-wicket (hyphenation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cricket fielding positions use hyphens: 'mid-on', 'mid-off', 'mid-wicket'.

rubrics_metrics.name: morning (time references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'morning', 'evening', 'afternoon' because these change around the globe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'later on Monday'/'earlier on Tuesday' or GMT as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: names (first reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always use first and surnames at first reference in results and copy. Use surnames at second reference except for Thai names (and note East Asian surname-first conventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: nationalities (spelling/usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write nationalities in full rather than abbreviating, except 'U.S.' for United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Britain' not 'United Kingdom' or 'Great Britain' where appropriate. Use 'The Netherlands' not 'Holland'; use 'Taiwan' not 'Chinese Taipei'. Distinguish North and South Korea.

rubrics_metrics.name: news conference (terminology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'news conference' rather than 'press conference' as the latter implies non-print media are excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: off-spinner (cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated bowler type: 'off-spinner'.

rubrics_metrics.name: OK (capitalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'OK' (capitalized), not 'ok' or 'okay'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Olympiad (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Olympiad' only to mean the four-year period between Olympic Games.

rubrics_metrics.name: only (placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Only' should be placed immediately before the word or phrase it qualifies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Didier Drogba has been sent off only once...' not 'has only been sent off once.' 'Tiger Woods earned only seven billion dollars...' not 'only earned seven billion dollars...'

rubrics_metrics.name: pace bowler (cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'pace bowler' is a quick bowler in cricket who may not have the speed of a genuine fast bowler.

rubrics_metrics.name: pari-mutuel (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell as 'Pari-mutuel' (the French tote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not 'Paris-mutuel'.

rubrics_metrics.name: player of the year (lower case and storify)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower case for 'player of the year'. Many such awards exist, so storify only the most prestigious and say who is offering the accolade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'FIFA world player of the year Ronaldinho' — identify the awarding body.

rubrics_metrics.name: playoff (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word: 'playoff'.

rubrics_metrics.name: postpone vs cancel
rubrics_metrics.description: Matches or races called off but to be held later are 'postponed'; those scrapped completely are 'cancelled'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an event is postponed provide the new date if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portuguese/Brazilian player names (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portuguese and Brazilian players may be known by several names or nicknames; use the name by which they are commonly known in copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pele, Joao Pinto, Edu.

rubrics_metrics.name: practice/practise (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'practise' as the verb and 'practice' as the noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Maria Sharapova practised...' but 'Sharapova hurt her knee in practice...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Premier League (capitalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Premier League' (upper case P and L) for the English top division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primera Liga (naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Primera Liga' for the Spanish first division in soccer.

rubrics_metrics.name: prize money (format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write as two words: 'prize money'.

rubrics_metrics.name: quarter-final (hyphenation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated: 'quarter-final'.

rubrics_metrics.name: rack vs wrack
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Nerve-racking'/'racked with pain' use 'rack'; 'wrack' is used only for seaweed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The injured Owen was racked with pain.' Use 'wrack' only for seaweed contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: racket (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'racket', not 'racquet'.

rubrics_metrics.name: record (avoid 'new record')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'new record' as tautological; any record time/distance is by definition new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Asafa Powell set a world 100 metres record …' not 'set a new world record …'

rubrics_metrics.name: reigning (avoid redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Reigning' is redundant; 'reigning champions' are simply 'champions'.

rubrics_metrics.name: repeat vs repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'repetition' as the noun and 'repeat' as the verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'tried to avoid a repetition of the tiebreak blunder' not 'tried to avoid a repeat'.

rubrics_metrics.name: repechage (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contest between runners-up usually for a place in the final, especially in rowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: rugby positions (word run-together)
rubrics_metrics.description: Run two-word rugby position names together: flyhalf, scrumhalf, fullback. Soccer positions are separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also acceptable: tighthead prop, inside centre, loosehead prop, hooker.

rubrics_metrics.name: St (abbreviation for saint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'St' without a full point for 'Saint'.

rubrics_metrics.name: seasons (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'seasons' because it can cause confusion between northern and southern hemispheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use alternatives like 'close-season transfer' or give the month.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid 'saw' construction ('see' guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid giving inanimate objects the power of sight in sports copy (e.g. 'The game saw Steve McClaren...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tighter phrasing: 'The game was Steve McClaren's first as England coach.' Use active verbs for people: 'Lionel Messi shot wide.'

rubrics_metrics.name: semi-final (hyphenation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated: 'semi-final'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serie A (capitalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Serie A' for the Italian first division in soccer.

rubrics_metrics.name: set point (tennis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write as two words: 'set point'.

rubrics_metrics.name: set to (avoid weak phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'looks set to' as an unnatural phrase; use 'will' (sourced) or 'could/may/might/is preparing' as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sir (avoid titles in sports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use honorific 'Sir' or titles in sports reporting; use plain names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also 'honorifics' guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: ski vs sky (verbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'ski' as the verb for winter sports and 'sky' for hitting a ball high in cricket/baseball.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Kostelic skied the Sestriere course' vs 'Gilchrist skyed the ball to long leg'.

rubrics_metrics.name: soccer positions (formatting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write soccer position names as two words: wing back, centre half, full back, centre forward (except 'goalkeeper').

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish names (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spanish and South American players may be known by full names, single names, or nicknames; use the name in common use for the player.

rubrics_metrics.name: sponsors (use and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should not act as billboards for sponsors; sponsor names may be used within strict criteria related to common media usage and necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Team names: avoid sponsor names where sponsorship may change (exceptions: teams that began as works sides or where sponsorship is the only identity). Events: drop sponsor name where event is clear without it; include sponsor when the event would otherwise need an invented name. Rankings/statistics: use sponsor names only where necessary to indicate legitimate source (e.g. Reuters golf rankings). Avoid sponsors' names on domestic leagues that can be described by category (e.g. English Premier League).

rubrics_metrics.name: square leg (cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fielding position: two words 'square leg'; hyphenate when used adjectivally ('square-leg umpire').

rubrics_metrics.name: stadiums (plural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'stadiums', not 'stadia'.

rubrics_metrics.name: star/superstar (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid calling sports personalities 'star' or 'superstar'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise and factual rather than hyperbolic.

rubrics_metrics.name: straight (British phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use British English phrasing 'three successive wins' instead of American 'three straight wins'.

rubrics_metrics.name: stretcher (do not verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'stretcher' as a verb; say 'was carried off', not 'stretchered off'.

rubrics_metrics.name: team mate (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write as two words: 'team mate'.

rubrics_metrics.name: teams (plural usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat 'teams' and 'clubs' as plural nouns (they are plural) except in American sport headlines and some headline conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example headlines and copy guidance provided; maintain plural agreement in sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: test (lower case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower case 'test' when referring to cricket and rugby union test matches.

rubrics_metrics.name: third man (cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fielding position: two words 'third man'.

rubrics_metrics.name: tiebreak (tennis)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word: 'tiebreak'.

rubrics_metrics.name: titles of sports events (capitalization rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower case for generic words (sport names, junior, men's, women's, championship, tournament, meeting, match, test, race, game etc.). Use upper case for the formal title of an event (e.g. French Open tennis championships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use singular 'championship' when one title is at stake and plural 'championships' for more than one. Place the sport name before 'championship/tournament' when appropriate (e.g. U.S. Open tennis championships; U.S. Open golf championship).

rubrics_metrics.name: topspin (tennis)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word: 'topspin'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tri-nations (formatting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names: 'Tri-nations' (upper case T, hyphen, lower case n) for the southern hemisphere rugby competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: UEFA (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'UEFA' (Union of European Football Associations) always in capitals and as a singular noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'UEFA said it would …'

rubrics_metrics.name: v (fixture notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'v' (not 'versus' or 'vs') to describe a fixture.

rubrics_metrics.name: veteran (avoid overuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid calling someone a 'veteran' — be precise about age or experience instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the competitor's age or the number of tournaments contested where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: West Indies (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'West Indies', not 'The West Indies' (use 'Windies' only in headlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: wicketkeeper (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word: 'wicketkeeper'.

rubrics_metrics.name: wicketkeeper-batsman (hyphenation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated: 'wicketkeeper-batsman'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: a cricketer who is a recognised batsman but also fulfils a wicketkeeping role when fielding.

rubrics_metrics.name: winter (avoid seasonal terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using seasons (winter, summer) because they differ between hemispheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the month instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: wrack vs rack (spelling/meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Wrack' is for seaweed; 'rack' for 'racked with pain' and similar constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The injured Owen was racked with pain.' Use 'wrack' only for seaweed contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: yards (measurement policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use metres except in golf and American sports where yards, feet, inches continue to be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cricket: include statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Cricket is rich in statistics and any cricket reporting should include such statistics (bowling, batting, wicketkeeping, fielding, partnerships, venues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use resources like cricinfo and Wisden for stats and records. Cross-check figures with scoreboards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cricket: report bowling, strokes, fielding positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Cricket reporting should include details of the type of bowling (fast, medium pace, leg spin, off spin) and some strokes (cut, sweep, pull, drive), and fielding positions to describe dismissals or shot placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fielding positions (slips, short leg, silly mid-on, third man, long leg, deep point) to describe action accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cricket: weather, pitch and scoring context
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention the weather and state of the pitch as they can favor bowlers or batsmen; scoring rate is particularly relevant in one-day matches limited to (usually) 50 overs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these contextual factors in storytelling as they affect match progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cricket: coverage schedule and story types
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuters covers test matches and one-day internationals with specific story expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tests: preview ~36 hours before, spot stories on injuries leading up, toss and teams, scores/scoreboards at lunch and tea intervals and at close; correspondents should write a lunch story (~200 words), update at tea, quick update at close, followed by a wrap and a quotes piece; for major matches more frequent updates/highlights may be required. For one-day internationals: generally no preview; run toss and teams, update at end of innings, quick result update, lead and quotes. Sidebars and features (venues, history, characters, interviews) are welcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cricket: style points (scores and slugs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within a story, write out scores and bowlers' figures in prose (e.g. '25 for two' or 'two for 25'); use abbreviations like '2-25' in results/stats boxes. Slugs should include a masterslug for tours (touring side or SERIES/TRIANGULAR/ASHES conventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check figures in copy with the scoreboard; partnerships should tally with fall-of-wicket figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Golf: avoid minutiae; story focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Golf writers should not get bogged down in hole-by-hole minutiae; look for the unusual, masterly, colourful, or luckless to make good stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too much jargon slows the flow; seek human-interest and narrative angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Golf: tournament basics and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Most tournaments are strokeplay over four rounds; the four 'majors' are U.S. Masters, U.S. Open, British Open, U.S. PGA. Tournaments usually run Thursday-Sunday with cuts after two rounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For coverage provide previews, mid-round stories, wraps at end of each round, sidebars on players; London Sports Desk will advise levels. Coverage expanded for majors and Ryder Cup with stats, profiles, course description and features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Golf: style points and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard golf terms and spellings (par, birdie, eagle, albatross, bogey, double-bogey, triple-bogey; 'caddie' spelled with 'ie'; 'playoff' one word; 'prize money' two words; 'tee shot' two words; 'approach shot' two words; 'leaderboard' one word; 'matchplay' and 'strokeplay' one word; 'wildcard' one word).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tournament players may carry no more than 14 clubs; list of typical clubs provided. Golf is the only sport for which Reuters uses imperial measurements (yards, feet, inches) in copy. Reuters number style (spell out one to nine, use figures from 10 upward) applies to hole-numbering and par-values. Hyphenate par description when used adjectivally ('one-under-par 70').

rubrics_metrics.name: Motor racing: qualifying and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Cars must qualify for each Formula One race; pole position determined in qualifying the day before (usually Saturday). Qualifying and technical rules may change season to season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main preview with stats/background normally runs early on Wednesday (Tuesday for Monaco). Run spot stories daily up to race; cover practice and qualifying; during a race file only for exceptional incidents; afterwards file urgent winner, fast timings, updates, interviews and sidebars. Sports Desk seeks Formula One-related stories between races.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motor racing: style points and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specified spellings/capitalization (Formula One cap, 'Paddock', 'Scrutineering', 'Tyres' not 'tires' except US copy). 'Lights' signal start when they go out. 'Laps' include formation lap pre-race. Use correct plural/capitalization for 'Grand Prix' and avoid using engine make in team titles (describe as 'Mercedes-powered McLaren cars' only when relevant). Include terms like 'ballast', 'plank or skid block', 'marshals' (one 'l'), 'traction control', 'telemetry', 'apex'. Flags: chequered, yellow, red, blue meanings listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motor racing: other races
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuters covers Le Mans 24-hour with updates every ~4 hours and the big U.S. races (Indianapolis 500, Daytona 500) with previews/running stories/interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other motor races are covered when newsworthy (big accident, death, destruction, unusual incident).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soccer: coverage scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuters covers domestic league football, continental club football, friendlies and internationals, major youth competitions and spans FIFA/UEFA and other confederation matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confederation acronyms (UEFA, AFC, CAF, CONCACAF, CONMEBOL, OFC) with brief explanations. Follow FAs and leagues for discipline, transfers, refereeing, TV rights, sponsorship, finance, corruption and match-fixing. Club business and financial stories may require equities/general news codes as well as sports codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soccer: avoid free publicity and emphasise sports angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid free publicity, celebrity hype or sleaze; stories about players should have a sports news angle rather than pure promotional content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human interest, interviews and offbeat angles score if they have sporting relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soccer: injuries, hooliganism and off-field stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Injuries and recovery (especially involving big clubs or internationals) fuel copy; violence and hooliganism, crowd surges, accidents and stand collapses should be storified and covered even if league is not regularly followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security, police tactics and disorder produce strong copy; genuine disorder and injuries warrant coverage.
